title: Innu leaders cry foul over use of force in Sheshatshiu arrest; RCMP says man had weapon
summary: Harry Dyke was arrested Saturday night after police received a report of a disturbance involving a weapon, RCMP say.

image.caption: Innu Nation Grand Chief Jodie Ashini and Sheshatshiu Innu First Nation Chief Eugene Hart met with police on Monday. They're hoping trust in the community can be rebuilt, but are frustrated to have the same conversation again. (John Harris/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New
Harry Dyke was arrested Saturday night after police received a report of a disturbance involving a weapon, RCMP say.
Harry Dyke says his mobility issues prevented him from following police orders
First Nations leaders in Sheshatshiu, N.L., came out of a meeting with RCMP officials with a familiar frustration following an arrest that sparked protests in the community.
"It was heartbreaking," Innu Nation Grand Chief Jodie Ashini said in reference to a surveillance video of the arrest.
"It was definitely … way too much aggression," said Ashini.

Harry Dyke of Sheshatshiu was arrested Saturday night after police received a report of a disturbance involving a weapon, according to a Monday afternoon statement from the RCMP. The force said officers seized a weapon.

In footage captured by a Ring doorbell camera in the area that night, a metallic clang can be heard as an officer appears to run at Dyke, knocking him down. Dyke told CBC News he was carrying a steel bar to ward off wild dogs.
He was also charged for resisting arrest.

Dyke is a burn victim and can't lift his hands over his head, according to Ashini. He can be heard in the video from Betty Sillitt’s home saying, "I can’t! I’m handicapped!" when police seemingly ask him to put his hands up.

Harry Dyke, right, was charged Saturday night with carrying a dangerous weapon and resisting arrest. He says he carried a steel bar with him that night to ward off wild dogs, and his mobility issues prevented him from raising his hands as directed. (John Harris/CBC)

In an interview with CBC News, Dyke said despite the charge, he doesn’t feel he resisted arrest. He said he couldn’t follow the instructions due to his mobility issues and instead put his hands behind his back to surrender.
That’s when Dyke said he was tackled.
"It’s not good how they [treated] me," said Dyke.
Outrage, frustration in Sheshatshiu following arrest by RCMP
Protesters boarded up RCMP detachment, yelled at police
Protesters showed up at the local RCMP detachment shortly after the arrest Saturday night. A video shows people drilling pieces of wood over several of the building’s entrances.

In a video of the demonstration taken by Florence Milley, someone behind the camera can be heard shouting, "Where’s Harry to? We're not scared!" while protesters gathered around RCMP officers exiting the building.

At one point during the video, it appears one of the people pushes an officer, while saying “Get out of here!” The officer turns around quickly at the touch, but he and the other officer keep walking away from the large group, as the person behind the camera continues to shout, “We’re not scared!”
The officers get into an RCMP vehicle and drive away.
The RCMP’s statement said people were still inside the building at the time, and three police vehicles were also damaged Saturday night.
Protesters appeared to barricade doors to the RCMP detachment in Sheshatshiu Saturday night. (Submitted by Florence Milley)
In the same written statement, the RCMP said it’s working to "identify opportunities for constructive conversations and measures that can improve public safety.”

Ashini and Sheshatshiu Innu First Nation Chief Eugene Hart met with police at the detachment Monday following the past weekend’s events — and some community members followed. They said they want them to take immediate action in increasing trust with Indigenous communities like theirs.
"We shouldn’t have to do their work for them," said Hart. "There’s zero communication.”

The leaders asked police to look into de-escalation tactics and to consider hiring an Innu liaison. Hart said the next time an officer is hired in Sheshatshiu, he and Ashini will sit in on the interview.
Ashini said if police are familiar with the community they’re serving, incidents like these could be prevented.
"We walk different roads … you need to understand who we are, how we live," said Ashini.
The grand chief said she and Hart have been down this road with police before. Just months ago, Innu leadership accused Mounties of using excessive force in a different arrest.
"It’s just déjà vu. You feel like you’re sitting in the same chair, saying the same thing," said Ashini.
